text: Job Displacement – What the Numbers Indicate (1)Disruption is Real: •Studies by organizations like the World Economic Forum (WEF) suggest significant churn in jobs due to AI and automation. –The WEF’s Future of Jobs 2023 report estimates that about 83 million jobs could be eliminated globally by 2027, while 69 million new jobs may be created, yielding a net loss of 14 million jobs (about 2% of current employment). –This marks a shift from earlier projections that AI might create more jobs than it destroys – recent data indicates a potential net negative in the short term as specific roles become redundant. 134

Job Displacement – What the Numbers Indicate (2)Who is Affected: •Jobs consisting of routine or repetitive tasks are most vulnerable. –For example, roles like data entry clerks, customer service reps (with AI chatbots handling inquiries), assembly line workers (with robotics), and basic accounting/bookkeeping are seeing declines. –A McKinsey study in 2023 projected that by 2030, nearly 30% of hours worked in the US could be automated, with lower-wage roles up to 14 times more likely to need career changes than higher-wage roles. –This suggests a risk of widening inequality if low-skill workers are displaced faster. 135

Job Displacement – What the Numbers Indicate (3)AI “White-Collar Automation”: •Significantly, AI is now automating some cognitive tasks (drafting reports, coding, legal document review), which means even professions like junior lawyers, programmers, or journalists will experience shifts. –Ex. After GPT-4’s release, some companies announced slowing hiring for specific content production roles, using AI to boost output instead. –However, outright replacement in skilled jobs is still limited – often, AI handles parts of the job. 136

Job Displacement – What the Numbers Indicate (4)Geographic and Sector Variance: •Advanced economies could see greater automation effects (an IMF study finds ~60% of jobs in advanced countries are highly exposed to AI vs ~40% in emerging economies), because more roles are digitized. •Sectors like manufacturing and finance are heavily impacted (e.g., manufacturing may lose up to 20 million jobs worldwide to robots by 2030, according to Oxford Economics ). •Conversely, sectors with human-intensive interaction (healthcare, education) may see net job growth as demand rises and AI serves as a tool rather than a replacement. 137

Job Creation and Transformation – New Roles in the Age of AI(1)New Categories of Jobs: •AI is giving rise to entirely new roles that barely existed a few years ago. –Examples include AI/ML Specialists, data scientists, AI ethics officers, prompt engineers (who craft inputs to guide AI systems), AI model trainers/tuners, and ML-Ops (machine learning operations) professionals responsible for deploying and monitoring AI systems. –The WEF reports strong growth in demand for these roles – specifically, jobs for AI and Machine Learning Specialists are projected to increase by ~40% by 2027. –Also in demand are data analysts and digital transformation specialists who help companies integrate AI. 138

Job Creation and Transformation – New Roles in the Age of AI(2)Augmentation Roles: •Many existing occupations are evolving to incorporate AI. –Ex. Doctors now work with AI diagnostic tools (so knowledge of AI is becoming part of the job), –Journalists may need to supervise AI content generators, and customer support reps might primarily handle escalations that the AI couldn’t. –This means job descriptions are shifting – requiring a blend of domain expertise and AI tool proficiency. 139

Job Creation and Transformation – New Roles in the Age of AI(3)AI as a Job Creator: •While some jobs vanish, AI can also increase productivity, leading to business growth and new job openings. –Ex. the e-commerce boom driven by AI recommendations has created numerous jobs in logistics, digital marketing, and related fields. –Another angle: as AI automates tasks, some companies reinvest savings into expansion or new products, which can create different jobs (the classic “productivity dividend”). –Approximately 49% of companies in a WEF survey expect AI to be a net job creator in their firm, versus 23% expecting a net loss. –These expectations suggest many businesses plan to redeploy workers to higher-value activities alongside AI. 140

Job Creation and Transformation – New Roles in the Age of AI(3)Hybrid Jobs: •A notable trend is the rise of “hybrid” jobs that combine skill sets – e.g., marketing professionals now need data analytics skills (to work with AI-driven analytics), and HR specialists might need to be adept with AI recruitment tools. •This blending of roles often makes jobs more interesting and strategic, even if fewer pure specialist roles remain.Gig and Entrepreneurial Opportunities: •AI lowers barriers to entry in some fields, enabling small startups or freelancers to do work that required large teams (e.g., a single person with AI tools can develop an app or create content at scale). •This can lead to more entrepreneurship and gig work – some displaced workers may become freelancers offering AI-augmented services (like an architect using AI to generate design options quickly).141

Augmentation Over Replacement – The Human-AI Team (1)Expert Views: •Suggest AI will change jobs more than it completely automates them. •AI pioneer Andrew Ng has noted, “AI won’t replace people, but people who use AI will replace people who don’t”. •This implies that workers augmented by AI become significantly more productive, potentially outperforming those who don’t leverage these tools. 142

Augmentation Over Replacement – The Human-AI Team (2)Productivity Boost Evidence: •A study at a large company found that customer support agents given an AI assistant (which suggested responses and knowledge articles in real time) became 14% more productive on average. •Notably, the biggest improvement was among less experienced workers – AI helped novices “catch up” in skill to veteran agents faster. –This suggests AI can act as a skill equalizer, raising overall team performance and reducing errors, rather than eliminating the agents. –Job satisfaction in that case also rose, as agents could handle issues more confidently. 143

Augmentation Over Replacement – The Human-AI Team (3)Task vs Job Automation: •Most jobs are a bundle of tasks, some of which are automatable, others require human qualities (creativity, interpersonal skills, judgment). •For instance, an accountant’s routine bookkeeping can be done by AI, but advising clients on complex financial strategies or navigating ambiguous regulations still needs a human touch. •Thus, we see task automation – AI handling 20–30% of a given job’s tasks, which can transform the job but not remove it. •Economist Erik Brynjolfsson emphasizes that augmenting workers yields better outcomes than trying to replace them entirely. 144

Augmentation Over Replacement – The Human-AI Team (4)Job Satisfaction and Enrichment: •When mundane tasks are offloaded, many workers can focus on more meaningful aspects of their jobs (strategy, creative problem solving, interpersonal interaction). •The hope is that AI could reduce drudgery (like paperwork for doctors or coding boilerplate for developers), making work more engaging. –However, there is a risk that some employers might increase work targets since AI makes tasks more efficient.–So it’s crucial to redesign workflows thoughtfully, not just to squeeze more output per worker. 145

Augmentation Over Replacement – The Human-AI Team (5)Upskilling to Collaborate with AI: •The paradigm is shifting to “human-AI collaboration.” •New training programs are teaching workers how to use AI tools in their domain.–Ex. Courses for lawyers on AI research tools, or factory workers on overseeing AI-controlled machines. •This way, employees become “AI-literate” and can truly partner with the technology, making themselves indispensable in the new workflow. 146

Reskilling and Workforce Development Initiatives (1)Mass Reskilling Imperative: •To adapt to AI disruption, continuous learning is critical. •Both governments and companies have launched major reskilling initiatives. •The World Economic Forum’s Reskilling Revolution initiative aims to provide better skills and education to 1 billion people by 2030, rallying public-private partnerships globally. •This includes online training platforms, vocational programs in digital skills, and efforts to lower barriers for people to enter tech fields. 147

Reskilling and Workforce Development Initiatives (2)Corporate Programs: •Big tech companies (IBM, Google, Microsoft) offer free or subsidized AI and data science courses, recognizing that a more AI-skilled general workforce ultimately expands their own talent pool and market. –Ex. IBM’s “New Collar” initiative trains non-degree holders in tech skills, focusing on areas like cloud and AI. –Amazon pledged $700M to upskill 100,000 employees for more advanced jobs (from fulfillment center workers learning IT support to coders learning machine learning). 148

Reskilling and Workforce Development Initiatives (3)Government Policies: •Many governments have begun integrating AI into their national skills strategies. –Singapore launched AI apprenticeship programs and an “AI for Everyone” literacy campaign to familiarize citizens with basic AI concepts. –The European Union’s Digital Europe programme allocates funding for advanced digital skills development, including AI. –The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 in the US not only funded semiconductor manufacturing but also authorized workforce development in AI and other emerging tech . –Community colleges and universities are updating curricula (introducing AI modules into business, healthcare, and even liberal arts programs to ensure future graduates are AI-aware). 149

Reskilling and Workforce Development Initiatives (4)Targeted Transition Support: •Specific sectors are receiving help – e.g., coal miners in some regions are being offered data analytics training to transition into tech jobs, recognizing that automation and decarbonization are shrinking mining jobs. •Similarly, call center workers might be retrained to manage AI-driven customer service platforms. Some proposals suggest “training vouchers” or tax credits for mid-career workers to encourage continuous skill upgrades.–The scale of reskilling needed is enormous and time-sensitive – training millions in new skills before they lose jobs or shortly thereafter. –There’s also an age and education divide: older or less-educated workers may find it harder to pivot to new careers. –Thus, programs need to be inclusive, offering, for example, paid time off for training, accessible course design, and job placement support. •Best results occur when training is closely aligned with industry needs (e.g., apprenticeships where companies commit to hiring participants). 150

Policy Responses and Labor Market Adjustments (1)•Labor Policy Innovations: Policymakers are exploring various strategies to cushion AI’s impact. Some key ideas:–Stronger Social Safety Nets: Enhancing unemployment benefits or creating “wage insurance” so if workers have to take lower-paying jobs after displacement, part of the gap is covered temporarily.–Job Transition Programs:–Lifelong Learning Accounts: –Work-Time Reduction: –Universal Basic Income (UBI): A more radical idea often discussed is UBI – regular cash payments to all citizens – to provide a floor if job displacement becomes very high. •However, UBI remains politically debated and would require high taxation or reallocation of resources.151

Policy Responses and Labor Market Adjustments (2)Collective Bargaining and Worker Voice: •Unions and worker groups are pushing to have a say in how AI is implemented in workplaces. –For instance, the new Hollywood writers’ contract (WGA, 2023) included guardrails on the use of AI in scriptwriting (ensuring writers aren’t paid less or replaced by AI). –Similar conversations are happening in other sectors. –In Germany, works councils are involved when companies introduce algorithms that affect employees. –This ensures AI augmentation happens in a way that workers feel is fair and transparent. 152

Policy Responses and Labor Market Adjustments (3)Economic Productivity and New Jobs: •AI-driven productivity growth could lead to cheaper goods/services and new market opportunities (analogous to how the internet created entirely new industries). •Governments are thus also investing in AI R&D and encouraging industries (through tax incentives or grants) to adopt AI, hoping to spawn job growth in tech, manufacturing of AI hardware, etc. –For example, the US National AI Initiative coordinates federal investments in AI research and education to maintain leadership and job creation in AI fields.•The consensus is that while AI will disrupt labor markets, thoughtful policy and a commitment to worker support can shape a future where AI boosts prosperity without leaving large groups behind. •It requires foresight (preparing workers in advance), inclusion (ensuring all demographics can access new opportunities), and adaptability (policies that can adjust as the tech and its impacts evolve). 153

Adapting to the AI Labor Revolution (1)•AI is undeniably changing the job landscape – some jobs will go away, many will change, and new ones will emerge. •The net effect in the medium term could be slight job loss or neutral, but with significant transitions required. The mantra for workers and businesses alike should be “adaptability”. For Workers: •Embrace lifelong learning and be proactive in gaining skills in collaboration with AI. –Skills like complex problem-solving, creativity, and interpersonal communication will remain in demand – combined with digital and AI literacy, they make for resilient careers. –The most “AI-proof” roles often involve empathy (teachers, nurses), strategic thinking, or dexterity in unpredictable environments – but even those jobs will use AI tools, so being able to work alongside AI is critical.154

Adapting to the AI Labor Revolution (2)For Employers: •Invest in your workforce – it can be more cost-effective to upskill existing employees for new tech-driven roles than to lay off and hire new. Moreover, a loyal, skilled workforce is a competitive asset. •Implement AI gradually and with employee input, focusing on augmentation and quality improvement rather than solely on headcount reduction. •Many companies find that AI allows them to scale up business and actually hire more people (in new areas) rather than simply cut costs – this growth mindset can benefit both the company and the labor market. 155

Adapting to the AI Labor Revolution (3)For Policymakers: •The time to act is now. Policies that prepare the workforce and protect those caught in transitions will determine whether AI leads to prosperity or pain. •Countries that get this right could enjoy an “AI dividend” – higher productivity, new industries, and a workforce with better jobs (more creative, less drudgery). •Those who lag may face social challenges of unemployment and inequality. •AI will be as transformative to work in the 21st century as mechanization was in the 20th. –History shows that although there can be turbulence, ultimately, new technology has led to new opportunities and higher living standards. –With conscious effort to guide AI’s integration into labor, we can aim for the same – a future where jobs are not eliminated but transformed, and where humans, augmented by AI, achieve more than ever before.156
AI in Marketing (Segmentation, Personalization, Analytics, Customer Journey) 157

AI: The New Engine of MarketingMarketing Transformation: •Artificial intelligence has become integral to modern marketing, powering everything from how companies understand customers to how they communicate with them. Core promise: •AI can analyze vast customer data to find patterns no human could, enabling exact customer segmentation, predictive analytics for campaign outcomes, and personalized content delivered at the optimal moment in the customer journey. •The result is marketing that is more targeted, efficient, and often more effective. •This presentation examines key AI applications in marketing.–Segmentation, dynamic content creation, predictive analytics, customer journey optimization –Along with real-world results and considerations for implementation.158 AI在营销中的核⼼承诺：更精准的理解顾客，预测营销活动效果，⽣成个性化内容，在客户旅程的最佳时机触达顾客

AI-Driven Customer Segmentation – Knowing Your Audience(s) (1)From Macro to Micro-Segments: •Traditional marketing segmented customers by broad demographics. •AI enables dynamic segmentation that accounts for real-time behaviors and nuanced attributes. •By analyzing purchase history, browsing behavior, social media interactions, and other data, AI creates microsegments that reflect customers’ current interests and intent. –Ex. an AI might identify a segment like “tech-savvy urban parents who browsed eco-friendly products in the last 2 weeks” –A grouping that is far more specific (and actionable) than classic segments like “18–34 urban males.” 159

AI-Driven Customer Segmentation – Knowing Your Audience(s) (2)Attitudinal + Behavioral Data: •Advanced approaches combine attitudinal segmentation (values, motivations gleaned from surveys or social media sentiment) with behavioral data (actual actions taken). –This gives a 3D view of the customer. –ZS Associates notes that this integration results in segments that can be updated in real-time as customer behavior changes. •If a customer’s pattern shifts (say they start looking at luxury items), AI can reassign them to a different segment promptly, ensuring marketing stays relevant. 160

AI-Driven Customer Segmentation – Knowing Your Audience(s) (3)Personalization at Scale: •With microsegments, marketers can tailor messaging and offers much more closely to what each group cares about. •AI systems often generate segment-specific content automatically. –For instance, an e-commerce retailer’s AI could send personalized home page banners –One customer sees “Recommended hiking gear for your next adventure ,” while another sees “New arrivals in smart home gadgets” based on their segment profile. 161

AI-Driven Customer Segmentation – Knowing Your Audience(s) (4)•Amazon is famous for using AI segmentation to drive its “customers who bought X also bought Y” and personalized recommendations. •Another example: Starbucks uses AI in its loyalty app to segment customers by time-of-day preferences and flavor choices, then sends targeted promotions (e.g., an afternoon iced coffee discount to someone who usually buys in mornings – nudging a new habit). •These practices, fueled by AI analysis, have contributed to higher redemption and engagement rates. Outcome: •AI-driven segmentation helps marketers spend more efficiently – focusing on the right customers with the right message – and typically improves conversion rates since relevance is higher. •The Aberdeen Group found that companies using AI for segmentation/predictive analytics enjoyed a ~ 10% annual improvement in marketing ROI, compared to ~1.5% for non-users. 162

Predictive Analytics – Forecasting Customer Behavior (1)What is Predictive Marketing Analytics: •It’s using machine learning to analyze historical customer data and identify patterns that predict future outcomes. •Standard predictions include: likelihood of a customer to churn, lifetime value, propensity to buy a product, or best next offer. –Ex. A telecom might use AI to predict which customers are at high risk of cancelling (churn) in the next 3 months based on usage trends and service feedback, then target them with retention offers proactively. 163

Predictive Analytics – Forecasting Customer Behavior (2)Campaign Outcome Prediction: •AI can forecast how a campaign might perform before it’s launched. •By examining factors like past campaign performance, current market conditions, and target audience attributes, it can estimate key metrics (open rates, click-through, conversion). –Stat: One study found marketers using predictive analytics achieved a 10% YoY increase in marketing ROI compared to ~1-2% for those not using such tools – meaning predictive insights informed them where to allocate budget for best returns. 164

Predictive Analytics – Forecasting Customer Behavior (3)Resource Allocation: •AI helps in marketing mix modeling – determining the optimal allocation of budget across channels (TV , search, social, email, etc.). •These models consider diminishing returns and synergies. –For instance, an AI might suggest spending slightly less on Facebook and more on TikTok this quarter for a fashion brand’s target Gen-Z audience, forecasting higher total conversions. –Companies like Procter & Gamble have used AI to adjust their multi-billion-dollar ad budgets, reportedly seeing 30% efficiency gains while meeting targets.Lead Scoring: •In B2B marketing/sales, predictive models score incoming leads by their likelihood to convert into customers, helping sales teams focus on the hottest prospects. •This increases sales productivity and ensures marketing efforts (like nurturing campaigns) are appropriately directed.165

Predictive Analytics – Forecasting Customer Behavior (4)Real-Time Adjustments: •Predictive analytics isn’t one-and-done; models can update predictions continuously as new data comes in (e.g., if during a campaign an AI sees early response is higher than predicted from one segment, it might forecast higher final results and suggest reallocating more budget mid-campaign to capitalize on that). •This agility, guided by AI forecasts, maximizes campaign performance dynamically. Caution: •Predictions are probabilities, not certainties. •Marketing teams must interpret them wisely – understanding the why behind a prediction is crucial (some modern AI tools offer explainability, like which factors led the model to tag a customer as “likely buyer”). •Combining predictive analytics with human intuition and market knowledge yields the best results. 166

AI-Generated Content – Dynamic Creation for Marketing (1)Generative AI in Marketing: •Marketers are tapping AI to create content ranging from ad copy to personalized emails to product images. Copywriting: •NLP models can draft copy variations in seconds. •They can produce social media captions, blog outlines, and even entire product descriptions tuned to different tones (formal vs casual) or keywords (for SEO). •As mentioned earlier, JPMorgan Chase’s marketing partnership with an AI copy platform saw AI-written ads significantly outperform human ones in click-through. •Such successes have led many companies to integrate AI into their creative process – perhaps as a first draft generator that humans refine.167

AI-Generated Content – Dynamic Creation for Marketing (2)A/B Testing at Scale: •Instead of manually coming up with a few ad variants, AI can generate dozens of text and image combos. •Then, using multivariate testing, the AI itself can determine which variant resonates most with each audience segment. –Ex. An online retailer’s AI marketing system might generate 50 versions of a Facebook ad (varying headline, body text, image type) and then learn that Version 17 works best for young shoppers while Version 4 works for older ones, automatically serving each group their winning creative. –This hyper-optimization drives up overall engagement and conversion. 168

AI-Generated Content – Dynamic Creation for Marketing (3)Visual Content: •Generative adversarial networks (GANs) and similar tech can create product images or modify them. •E-commerce sites use AI to generate images of models wearing clothing in different styles or on other body types without needing endless photo shoots. •Some brands are also using AI to create personalized visuals in emails – e.g., an image that incorporates the customer’s name artistically, or location-specific imagery based on weather. –Coca-Cola’s AI platform, which allows for personalized ad image creation, is an example of leveraging consumer input and AI to yield unique, tailored visuals at scale. 169

AI-Generated Content – Dynamic Creation for Marketing (4)Scale and Speed: •The time and cost savings of AI content generation are huge – Deloitte estimated up to 2-3x more output for 40-70% less cost. •This means marketers can run more campaigns simultaneously or keep content fresher with rapid refresh cycles (important in social media, where content burnout is quick). 170

AI-Generated Content – Dynamic Creation for Marketing (5)Ensuring Brand Consistency: •One concern – with so much automated variation, how to ensure brand voice remains consistent? •Solutions include training AI on a company’s past high-performing content so it learns the style, and setting rules/guardrails (e.g., words to avoid, mandatory phrases, tone guidelines). •Advanced AI systems enable the upload of brand guidelines and generate content that aligns with them. •Grammarly Business’s tone-consistency features and other AI copy tools help enforce a unified voice. 171

AI-Generated Content – Dynamic Creation for Marketing (6)Human Oversight & Creativity: •Marketers report that AI frees them to focus on higher-level creative strategy – brainstorming campaign concepts, big ideas, and experiential marketing – while AI handles repetitive creative tasks and minor variations. •The creative team’s role shifts to curator/editor, steering AI and infusing the human spark where needed (since AI, while clever with patterns, doesn’t truly innovate on its own in a strategic sense). 172

Personalized Customer Journey – The Right Message at the Right Time (1)Journey Orchestration: •AI helps map and optimize the entire customer journey – from awareness to consideration to purchase to retention. •It can analyze how customers move through funnels (which touchpoints they hit, where they drop off) and identify opportunities to intervene with the perfect message or offer. –Example: AI might find that a user visited a product page twice but didn’t buy – it could trigger a personalized follow-up, like a push notification or email with a limited-time discount on that product to spur conversion. Predictive Customer Lifetime Value (CLV): •AI can project CLV for each customer and then tailor the journey accordingly. •High-CLV customers might get white-glove treatment (e.g., personal shopper outreach), whereas lower CLV ones get more automated nurturing – optimizing resource allocation. •Also, if AI predicts that a customer’s CLV could increase with cross-selling of a particular product, it will prompt marketing to introduce that at the right moment. 173

Personalized Customer Journey – The Right Message at the Right Time (2)Dynamic Content & Offers: •The content a customer sees on a website or app can now be fully AI-driven based on their profile and stage in the journey. –Ex. A first-time visitor might see an educational blog post or video (to build awareness), while a repeat visitor with items in cart sees a banner for “free shipping if you check out today.” –AI rules make these decisions, maximizing the chance of progressing that customer to the next stage. –As another example, Netflix’s AI not only recommends shows but even chooses which thumbnail image to show each user for the same show (e.g., highlighting the genre aspect a particular user likes – romance vs action) to increase click-through. 174

Personalized Customer Journey – The Right Message at the Right Time (3)Multi-Channel Coordination: •AI can ensure consistency and optimal timing across channels (email, SMS, social, app notifications). •If a customer ignores an email, AI might follow up days later via a different channel they’re more responsive to. •Or it might pause messaging to someone who just purchased (preventing an embarrassing scenario of “Are you still interested in X?” after they bought it – something simpler systems might miss). •This holistic view, often called “next best action” marketing, uses reinforcement learning to decide the best possible interaction at any point. 175

Personalized Customer Journey – The Right Message at the Right Time (4)Customer Experience & Satisfaction: •A personalized journey feels more relevant and less spammy to customers, often improving satisfaction and loyalty. –However, marketers must be careful not to cross the line into feeling invasive – personalization should feel helpful, not creepy. •Transparency (like allowing users to set preferences) can help. •Personalization can make marketing feel like a service. –Ex. A travel app’s AI might learn a user’s preferences and proactively suggest a curated weekend trip itinerary at a reasonable price – the user perceives this as value-add rather than an ad. 176

Personalized Customer Journey – The Right Message at the Right Time (4)Results: •Many companies have reported notable lifts using journey personalization: –Higher email open and conversion rates, improved retention, and even reduced marketing spend waste. •For one, PepsiCo’s AI-driven marketing mix model recommended reallocating 12% of its marketing budget, which led to a projected $53M annual revenue increase. –Demonstrating that optimizing the journey touchpoints and spend can directly impact the bottom line. 177
